Introduction to qualtdict

Yuhao Lin

Source: vignettes/qualtdict.Rmd
qualtdict.Rmd

A Qualtrics response download names its columns with identifiers such as QID12_3_TEXT, and what each identifier means is spread across several nested metadata objects: questions, choices, matrix items, loops, embedded data and scoring rules. Before any analysis, every column has to be matched back to that metadata, renamed, labelled and documented.

qualtdict does that mapping for you. From the survey metadata it builds a Variable Dictionary, one table describing every exported response column, which you can inspect, validate and share as a codebook. It then applies the dictionary to the responses downloaded through qualtRics, so that every column carries its variable name and labels.

The authors and contributors for this R package are not affiliated with Qualtrics, and Qualtrics does not offer support for this R package.

The workflow

  1. dict_generate() builds a Variable Dictionary from the survey metadata.
  2. dict_validate() reports Validation Findings in the dictionary.
  3. survey_fetch_labelled() downloads the responses and applies the dictionary, returning Labelled Survey Data.
  4. dict_split_blocks() and survey_split_blocks() give one view per Survey Block.

Steps 1 and 3 read your survey from Qualtrics and need API credentials. Your institution must allow API access, and it must be enabled for your account; the person who manages your Qualtrics account can give you your API token and base URL. Store them once with qualtrics_api_credentials(), which qualtdict re-exports from qualtRics:

library(qualtdict)

qualtrics_api_credentials(
  api_key = "<YOUR-QUALTRICS_API_KEY>",
  base_url = "<YOUR-QUALTRICS_BASE_URL>",
  install = TRUE
)

The example survey

This vignette uses glad_example, an example bundled with the package. It holds the metadata of a subset of the GLAD Study sign-up survey (four demographic questions, the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 blocks, six embedded data fields and two scoring variables), 20 synthetic responses, and the objects qualtdict produces from them.

library(qualtdict)

names(glad_example)
#> [1] "survey_metadata"      "survey_description"   "response_column_map" 
#> [4] "responses"            "dictionary"           "labelled_survey_data"

For your own survey, the calls below would download the metadata and the responses from Qualtrics. They are not run here; for the example survey they return exactly glad_example$dictionary and glad_example$labelled_survey_data, which the rest of this vignette uses.

survey_id <- "SV_XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX"

dict <- dict_generate(survey_id, variable_name = "question_name")
survey_dat <- survey_fetch_labelled(dict)
dict <- glad_example$dictionary
survey_dat <- glad_example$labelled_survey_data

The Variable Dictionary 

dict
#> # A tibble: 97 × 14
#>    response_column_id row_source qid     question_name variable_name block      
#>    <chr>              <chr>      <chr>   <chr>         <chr>         <chr>      
#>  1 QID1125_TEXT       question   QID1125 DEM.AGE.1.0   DEM.AGE.1.0   Demographi…
#>  2 QID1126            question   QID1126 DEM.COR.1.0   DEM.COR.1.0   Demographi…
#>  3 QID1126            question   QID1126 DEM.COR.1.0   DEM.COR.1.0   Demographi…
#>  4 QID1126            question   QID1126 DEM.COR.1.0   DEM.COR.1.0   Demographi…
#>  5 QID1126            question   QID1126 DEM.COR.1.0   DEM.COR.1.0   Demographi…
#>  6 QID1126            question   QID1126 DEM.COR.1.0   DEM.COR.1.0   Demographi…
#>  7 QID1127            question   QID1127 DEM.SEX.1.0   DEM.SEX.1.0   Demographi…
#>  8 QID1127            question   QID1127 DEM.SEX.1.0   DEM.SEX.1.0   Demographi…
#>  9 QID1147_1          question   QID1147 DEM.EDU.1.0   DEM.EDU.1.0   Demographi…
#> 10 QID1147_2          question   QID1147 DEM.EDU.1.0   DEM.EDU.1.0.1 Demographi…
#> # ℹ 87 more rows
#> # ℹ 8 more variables: question <chr>, item <chr>, level <chr>, label <chr>,
#> #   type <chr>, selector <chr>, sub_selector <chr>, content_type <chr>

Each row describes one downloaded response column, or one response level of it. The columns are:

  • response_column_id: the column name in the downloaded Qualtrics response file. This is how the dictionary is matched to your data.
  • row_source: what the column comes from (see below).
  • qid: the Qualtrics question the column belongs to, such as QID1125. One question can produce many response columns.
  • question_name: the question name set in the Qualtrics survey editor.
  • variable_name: the name the column gets in Labelled Survey Data. It is unique and safe for export.
  • block: the Survey Block the question belongs to.
  • question and item: the question text and, for matrix and multi-column questions, the text of the row or choice.
  • level and label: a response value and its label. A column with response options takes one row per option.
  • type, selector, sub_selector and content_type: the Qualtrics question type and its settings.

variable_name = "question_name" builds variable_name from the Qualtrics Question Name, repaired where needed so that every name is unique and export-safe. The original question_name stays in the dictionary.

A multi-select question gets one response column per choice, and a choice with a text box gets an extra _TEXT column:

dict[
  which(dict$qid == "QID1147"),
  c("response_column_id", "variable_name", "level", "label")
]
#> # A tibble: 8 × 4
#>   response_column_id variable_name level  label                                 
#>   <chr>              <chr>         <chr>  <chr>                                 
#> 1 QID1147_1          DEM.EDU.1.0   1      College or university degree          
#> 2 QID1147_2          DEM.EDU.1.0.1 1      A levels/AS levels or equivalent      
#> 3 QID1147_3          DEM.EDU.1.0.2 1      O levels/GCSEs or equivalent          
#> 4 QID1147_4          DEM.EDU.1.0.3 1      CSEs or equivalent                    
#> 5 QID1147_6          DEM.EDU.1.0.4 1      NVQ or HND or HNC or equivalent       
#> 6 QID1147_5          DEM.EDU.1.0.5 1      Other professional qualifications     
#> 7 QID1147_5_TEXT     DEM.EDU.1.0.6 5_TEXT Other professional qualifications_TEXT
#> 8 QID1147_-999       DEM.EDU.1.0.7 1      Prefer not to answer

A matrix question gets one response column per item, each with the scale’s levels:

dict[
  which(dict$qid == "QID127303424" & dict$level == "0"),
  c("response_column_id", "variable_name", "item")
]
#> # A tibble: 9 × 3
#>   response_column_id variable_name item

Row sources

Most rows come from survey questions, but Qualtrics also exports columns that are defined elsewhere in the survey. row_source says which:

  • question: a response to a survey question.
  • embedded_data: an Embedded Data Field set in the Survey Flow.
  • scoring: a Scoring Variable computed by Qualtrics scoring.
  • text_analysis: a Text-analysis Sidecar added by Qualtrics text analysis of a text response. The example survey has none.
table(dict$row_source)
#> 
#> embedded_data      question       scoring 
#>             6            89             2

dict[
  dict$row_source != "question",
  c("response_column_id", "row_source", "variable_name", "question")
]
#> # A tibble: 8 × 4
#>   response_column_id row_source    variable_name     question                   
#>   <chr>              <chr>         <chr>             <chr>                      
#> 1 Age                embedded_data Age               Embedded Data: Age         
#> 2 sex                embedded_data sex               Embedded Data: sex         
#> 3 PHQRaw             embedded_data PHQRaw            Embedded Data: PHQRaw      
#> 4 CurrentDepression  embedded_data CurrentDepression Embedded Data: CurrentDepr…
#> 5 GADRaw             embedded_data GADRaw            Embedded Data: GADRaw      
#> 6 CurrentGAD         embedded_data CurrentGAD        Embedded Data: CurrentGAD  
#> 7 SC_5gvP3Yxax8TWHcN scoring       GAD_7             Scoring Variable: GAD-7    
#> 8 SC_3rtKxr7Lzd9OHhX scoring       PHQ_9             Scoring Variable: PHQ-9

Validation Findings

dict_validate() returns a list with two components: validation_findings, one row per finding, and level_label_pairs, the distinct level-label codings of the survey’s questions.

validation <- dict_validate(dict)
names(validation)
#> [1] "validation_findings" "level_label_pairs"

validation$validation_findings[, c(
  "finding", "severity", "response_column_id", "original_candidate",
  "variable_name", "reason"
)]
#> # A tibble: 23 × 6
#>    finding   severity response_column_id original_candidate variable_name reason
#>    <chr>     <chr>    <chr>              <chr>              <chr>         <chr> 
#>  1 repaired… suggest… QID1147_2          DEM.EDU.1.0        DEM.EDU.1.0.1 dupli…
#>  2 repaired… suggest… QID1147_3          DEM.EDU.1.0        DEM.EDU.1.0.2 dupli…
#>  3 repaired… suggest… QID1147_4          DEM.EDU.1.0        DEM.EDU.1.0.3 dupli…
#>  4 repaired… suggest… QID1147_6          DEM.EDU.1.0        DEM.EDU.1.0.4 dupli…
#>  5 repaired… suggest… QID1147_5          DEM.EDU.1.0        DEM.EDU.1.0.5 dupli…
#>  6 repaired… suggest… QID1147_5_TEXT     DEM.EDU.1.0        DEM.EDU.1.0.6 dupli…
#>  7 repaired… suggest… QID1147_-999       DEM.EDU.1.0        DEM.EDU.1.0.7 dupli…
#>  8 repaired… suggest… QID127303424_2     PHQ.DEP.1.0        PHQ.DEP.1.0.1 dupli…
#>  9 repaired… suggest… QID127303424_3     PHQ.DEP.1.0        PHQ.DEP.1.0.2 dupli…
#> 10 repaired… suggest… QID127303424_4     PHQ.DEP.1.0        PHQ.DEP.1.0.3 dupli…
#> # ℹ 13 more rows

Each finding has a severity:

  • Suggestive findings are worth a look but leave the column’s data and identity sound. All findings here are of this kind: matrix items and multi-select choices share one Question Name, so their variable names are numbered, and the hyphens in PHQ-9 and GAD-7 are replaced so the scoring variables get export-safe names.
  • Definite findings mean the column cannot be interpreted or identified reliably: duplicate or unsafe final variable names, or level-label codings that are not one-to-one, such as two choices sharing one response code.

A clean result is a consistency check, not proof that the survey itself is correct.

dict_assert_valid() is the strict version for the definite findings that make labelling wrong or impossible, the Export-blocking level-label codings. It returns the dictionary invisibly when there are none, and raises an error naming the offending columns otherwise. The example dictionary passes:

dict_assert_valid(dict)

survey_fetch_labelled() runs this check before it downloads anything, so a dictionary that cannot be labelled fails before the download.

Export Variables are renamed from response_column_id to variable_name. By default survey_fetch_labelled() also keeps externalDataReference, startDate and endDate, and appends the response metadata columns recordedDate, ResponseId and Progress.

Choice columns carry their response options as value labels, and text and numeric columns carry the question text as a variable label:

attr(survey_dat$DEM.COR.1.0, "labels")
#>          England         Scotland            Wales Northern Ireland 
#>                1                2                3                4 
#>       Outside UK 
#>                5
attr(survey_dat$DEM.AGE.1.0, "label")
#> [1] "How old are you now?"

Packages that read these attributes, such as sjlabelled, can use them directly, for example to turn a coded column into a factor:

table(sjlabelled::as_label(survey_dat$DEM.COR.1.0))
#> 
#>          England         Scotland            Wales Northern Ireland 
#>                3                6                6                3 
#>       Outside UK 
#>                2

The Variable Dictionary used to build the data travels with it as the dict attribute, so the question and item text of every column stay at hand:

survey_dict <- attr(survey_dat, "dict")
unique(survey_dict[
  survey_dict$variable_name == "PHQ.DEP.1.0.2",
  c("variable_name", "item")
])
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   variable_name item                                                   
#>   <chr>         <chr>                                                  
#> 1 PHQ.DEP.1.0.2 Trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping too much

Labelled Export Findings

While applying the dictionary, survey_fetch_labelled() records Labelled Export Findings: for example, a dictionary column that is missing from the downloaded data. survey_export_findings() returns them. The example has none:

survey_export_findings(survey_dat)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 5
#> # ℹ 5 variables: finding <chr>, response_column_id <chr>, qid <chr>,
#> #   variable_name <chr>, reason <chr>

Download options

survey_fetch_labelled() calls qualtRics::fetch_survey() with the settings it needs to match columns to response_column_id: import_id = TRUE, label = FALSE, convert = FALSE and breakout_sets = TRUE. You may pass other fetch_survey() arguments, such as include_questions, but not ones that override those settings.

By default, variables with Validation Findings stay in the data. exclude_findings = "definite" drops the variables with definite findings, and exclude_findings = "validation" drops every variable with any finding:

survey_dat <- survey_fetch_labelled(
  dict,
  extra_columns = c("externalDataReference", "startDate", "endDate"),
  exclude_findings = "definite"
)

Survey Block views

dict_generate() returns one Variable Dictionary and survey_fetch_labelled() returns one data frame. To work with one Survey Block at a time, split them. Rows without a block, here the embedded data fields and scoring variables, are kept under "..unassigned".

dict_by_block <- dict_split_blocks(dict)
names(dict_by_block)
#> [1] "..unassigned" "Demographics" "GAD7"         "PHQ9"
unique(dict_by_block$PHQ9[, c("response_column_id", "variable_name")])
#> # A tibble: 10 × 2
#>    response_column_id variable_name
#>    <chr>              <chr>        
#>  1 QID127303424_1     PHQ.DEP.1.0  
#>  2 QID127303424_2     PHQ.DEP.1.0.1
#>  3 QID127303424_3     PHQ.DEP.1.0.2
#>  4 QID127303424_4     PHQ.DEP.1.0.3
#>  5 QID127303424_5     PHQ.DEP.1.0.4
#>  6 QID127303424_6     PHQ.DEP.1.0.5
#>  7 QID127303424_7     PHQ.DEP.1.0.6
#>  8 QID127303424_8     PHQ.DEP.1.0.7
#>  9 QID127303424_9     PHQ.DEP.1.0.8
#> 10 QID127303425       PHQ.EFT.1.0

data_by_block <- survey_split_blocks(survey_dat)
names(data_by_block)
#> [1] "..unassigned" "Demographics" "GAD7"         "PHQ9"
names(data_by_block$PHQ9)
#>  [1] "externalDataReference" "startDate"             "endDate"              
#>  [4] "PHQ.DEP.1.0"           "PHQ.DEP.1.0.1"         "PHQ.DEP.1.0.2"        
#>  [7] "PHQ.DEP.1.0.3"         "PHQ.DEP.1.0.4"         "PHQ.DEP.1.0.5"        
#> [10] "PHQ.DEP.1.0.6"         "PHQ.DEP.1.0.7"         "PHQ.DEP.1.0.8"        
#> [13] "PHQ.EFT.1.0"

By default each block’s data keeps externalDataReference, startDate and endDate so the blocks can be joined back together.

Semantic Names

If the Question Names in your survey are not good analysis names, ask for Semantic Names. They are generated from the question text, block information and response metadata, and need the suggested packages slowraker, SnowballC, stringi and tidyr. block_pattern turns each Survey Block name into a Block Prefix, which is prepended to the Semantic Names in that block so that variables from different blocks stay distinct:

block_pattern <- function(block) {
  substring(block, 1, 3)
}

dict <- dict_generate(
  survey_id,
  variable_name = "semantic_name",
  block_pattern = block_pattern,
  block_sep = "."
)

Semantic Names are best-effort readable conveniences. They are not stable across package versions or survey text changes, so do not treat them as permanent identifiers. For long text, Semantic Names select important words from ranked keywords and keep them in the order they appear in the text.

You can also preprocess the text used only for Semantic Name generation:

drop_intro_text <- function(dict) {
  dict$question <- sub("^Please answer: ", "", dict$question)
  dict
}

dict <- dict_generate(
  survey_id,
  variable_name = "semantic_name",
  semantic_name_preprocess = drop_intro_text
)

semantic_name_preprocess receives the full dictionary and runs only on the Semantic Name path. Temporary helper columns it creates are not included in the returned Variable Dictionary.

Learn more

The help page of each function, such as ?dict_generate or ?survey_fetch_labelled, documents its arguments in full.
